delete.description: Only its owner deletes it: a developer of it gets `owner_only`, and a member `member_only`. Its address, every share of it and its name go at once, so a deploy by that name makes a new app, with an empty disk. The operation succeeds once its host has stopped it and every gateway has dropped its address and shares and closed what was open to it. There's no trash and nothing restores it. While a deploy of it is under way, it's `app_busy`. Once it's deleted, sending it again answers `no_such_app`.

post.description: It takes the app's `app.toml` and the list of its files. The deploy runs in the background: check its operation, and upload every file when it asks. It writes each file at `/app/<path>` on the app's disk, replacing what's there and touching nothing else, runs the app's build there, and then starts the app on what its disk holds, even if the build failed. An image app's deploy lists no files: it pulls the image `app.toml` names and writes its files over the app's disk, deleting nothing, and an app whose disk was made for the other kind is `image_disk_mismatch`. Without `owner`, a deploy makes your app if you have none by its name, and with `new_app`, only then; with `owner`, the app must be one you're a developer of. While no host has room for a new app, a deploy that would make one is refused with `host_full` (503, retryable), and nothing is made: try again later. Apps that already exist still deploy.

get.description: It's what the app printed in its latest run and the run before, each at most its newest 1 MiB, with what its deploys and builds printed, and timed lines of the platform's own, starting `[anywhere `, saying when each run, deploy and build started and ended. With `follow`, the answer goes on with what the app prints next, through its restarts and deploys, for 30 minutes, when the platform ends it so the caller asks again. Without `follow`, the answer is the bytes as the app printed them, control characters and all, as `application/octet-stream`. With it, it's Server-Sent Events, `text/event-stream`: each part of the log is an event whose `data` is its bytes in base64 and whose `id` says where the log is after it, and a comment, `:`, comes after 20 seconds with nothing else, so a reader that hears nothing for a minute knows the connection dropped. A follow that ends, however it ends, is asked for again with `after` set to the last event's `id`, which sends only what follows it; a refusal then says if the caller's access ended. An `after` from before the platform restarted on the app's host reads the whole log again, after a `resume_lost` notice. `after=end` with `follow=false` answers only where the log ends now, as one empty event, for a caller to follow from.

All are set, or none: a name that isn't allowed, one given twice, a value that isn't, or a change past the app's limits refuses the whole request, naming the secret but never its value. It sets 1 to 100 secrets, in a request of at most 2103616 bytes, and leaves the app's others as they are. `create_app`, and sending it again, are as for one secret.

put.description: The app gets it as an environment variable of the same name. The name is an uppercase letter, then uppercase letters, digits and underscores, at most 64 characters. It can't be one the platform sets, HOME, PATH or PORT, or start with ANYWHERE_, which the platform keeps for its own. The value is UTF-8 text of 1 to 32768 bytes, without NUL characters, kept exactly as sent, in a request of at most 65536 bytes. An app has at most 100 secrets, of at most 1048576 bytes together, names and values. A running app restarts with its new secrets, and the operation succeeds once it has started again, as a deploy's does; an app that isn't running gets them when it next starts. An app you don't have is `no_such_app`, unless the request sets `create_app`, which makes only an app of your own, never with `owner`. A change to a web app that has no address yet succeeds with a warning that says how to give it one. Sending the same request again is safe, and restarts a running app once more.

put.description: The share names their verified email. A member uses it in their browser or with their agent token, as you do, and finds it in `GET /v1/shared-apps`. A developer can also deploy to it, run commands in it, read its logs and set its secrets, naming it with `owner`; only you share it. The app is told their username in the `Anywhere-User` header, and their role in `Anywhere-Role`, where you get `owner`. Someone with no account yet gets the app once they sign up with that email, and can be made a developer only once they have (`developer_needs_account`). Without `role`, a new share is a member's and an existing one keeps its role; another role changes it. An operation that makes someone a developer warns that developers read the app's secrets and that removing one doesn't undo what they changed. The operation succeeds once every gateway admits them as their role says, and, for a change to member, has closed what needed a developer. Sending it again is safe. The email goes in the body, never the path, so no request log holds it.

post.description: The deploy ends at once, failed with `deploy_cancelled`, so the app is no longer busy and the next deploy, secret change or delete goes ahead. Its owner and its developers cancel it. Nothing is rolled back and nothing is deleted: a deploy cancelled while it received its files or built leaves the files it had written, and the app starts again on what its disk holds; one cancelled while its app started leaves the app starting, or restarting after it exits, on its disk. Cancelling it again answers the same; a deploy that had already ended is `operation_ended`, and any other operation `operation_not_cancellable`.
